Отговаряйки на изследователския въпрос какви са характеристиките на съвременната среда за сигурност, авторът представя комплексния, хибриден характер на заплахите и новия стратегически контекст, в който агентите, следва да оперират; (cid:16)(cid:3)прави: 1/анализ на предизвикателствата пред ЕС и НАТО от икономическа, политическа и институционална гледна точка; 2/анализ на сътрудничеството и предизвикателствата във взаимодействието между двата съюза, показващи необходимост от: *допълнително засилване на сътрудничеството в областта на способностите; *по-висока степен на интегрираност и съвместимост на способностите и респективна допълняемост между двете организации; *повече доверие и обмен на разузнавателна информация; *разрешаване на проблема между Кипър и Турция, блокиращи практическото взаимодействие между НАТО и ЕС – Берлин плюс и отвъд споразуменията; *вземане под приоритетно внимание при стратегическо планиране: въпросите за тероризма, енергийната сигурност и свободния достъп до т.нар. глобални блага (море, въздух, космос и кибер) и 3/анализ на конкретни случаи – Либия, България и Украйна, показващи:*спецификата на заплахите от юг и изток; *липсата на ключови способности на ЕС; *възможни нови подходи за разширяването на (cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3) 477 Спигелере, С. и Р. Военни въпроси, Бъдещето на НАТО. 2006 <http://www.nato.int/docu/review/2006/issue2/bulgarian/military.html> (cid:3) 318 двата съюза (в Черноморския регион и пост съветското пространство – постигане първо на членство в ЕС и след това в НАТО; насочване приоритетно разширението на НАТО към страните от Западните Балкани и засилване от ЕС на Източното си партньорство, акцентирайки върху Украйна, Молдова и Грузия); (cid:16)(cid:3)тества емпирично чрез собствено социологическо изследване направените: теоретичен модел, препоръки и изводи, теза и хипотези в разработката. На база на гореизложеното авторът доказва тезата си за необходимостта от стратегическо преосмисляне на средата за сигурност и модернизация на Европейската стратегия за сигурност, посредством потвърждаване на хипотезите, че : 1. съвременната среда за сигурност е променена. Системата на международни отношения е със силна степен на неопределеност. Средата за сигурност се характеризира с: *комплексен характер на заплахите – асиметрични, хибридни, вътрешни и външни заплахи, характеризиращи се с висока степен на обвързаност помежду си, както и рискове, съдържащи нови компоненти – икономически, финансов, енергиен, екологичен, социален, правосъден; *различни възприятия и оценка на рисковете от държавите-членки, гражданите и вземащите решения в ЕС и НАТО. 2. съществува причинно-следствената връзка между промените в средата за сигурност и стратегическите документи на ЕС и НАТО, подкрепена от близо 94% от анкетираните, отговорили положително на въпроса, че поради динамичните промени на международната сцена, особено през последните три години, има необходимост от стратегическо преосмисляне на средата за сигурност, съпътствано от промяна на съществуващите стратегически документи на ЕС и НАТО. 3. съвременната среда за сигурност предполага по-добро взаимодействие между ЕС и НАТО. В контекста на позиционирането на ЕС като глобален актьор и способността му да отговори бързо на новите геостратегически реалности и предизвикателства, 72% от респондентите отбелязват необходимостта от тясно сътрудничество с НАТО. Всички анкетирани отбелязват необходимостта от подобряване на сътрудничеството между двата съюза, като най-висок процент, отбелязват приоритетно необходимостта от по-висока степен на интегрираност, съвместимост на способностите и допълняемост между съюзниците. Основните идеи и препоръки от настоящото изследване, извън вече емпирично тестваните, биха могли да бъдат обобщени по следния начин: 1. Очертаване на три потенциални сценария в контекста на сигурността и отбраната на ЕС: *ЕС да оптимизира своите способности в рамките на НАТО – т.е. ЕС да се превърне в своеобразен втори стълб на НАТО, като остава отворен въпросът за Кипър, Малта, които не са част от Алианса и неутралните страни Австрия, Швеция, Финландия, Ирландия, Швейцария, както и Дания, която не участва в ОПСО; *Военна интеграция в ЕС на „две скорости”, чрез възможността, която чл.I-41, т.6 от Лисабонския договор предоставя за постоянно структурирано сътрудничество между страните членки. Изискването в това сътрудничество е да участват само страните, притежаващи военни способности, които отговарят на високите критерии на съвременните мисии. Тя е свързана със сътрудничество с НАТО, изграждане на способности и по-активно включване на европейските държави в целия спектър от мисии на Алианса. *Самостоятелна европейска армия, като тук възникват два въпроса: *дали тя ще бъде по подобие на НАТО – т.е. няма да има единни обединени въоръжени сили, а ще разчита на националните военни сили на държавите-членки, като същевременно определи по подобие на Алианса индикатори за бюджетни разходи или *ще бъде изградена на (cid:3) 319 база визията на Жан Моне и Рене Плевен от 50-те години на XX век за Европейска отбранителна общност, имаща наднационален характер, с: *общи институции, въоръжени сили и бюджет; *единна система за военна подготовка и еднородно въоръжение, имащи изключително отбранителни цели на територията на ЕС. Кой от трите потенциални сценарии за ОПСО ще бъде развит зависи от трите ключови формули, разгледани в настоящата разработка – формулата за сила – ресурси, желание и умение да бъдат използвани, формулата за движение – път, скорост, време и формулата за устойчивост на вземаните решения – ясна стратегическа визия, политическа воля, не само на европейско, но и национално ниво и подкрепа на европейските граждани. Всеки един от предложените сценарии е свързан с определено ниво на интеграция. Предвид, обаче уникалността на Съюза, нещо като международна организация, нещо като федерация, „нещо като нищо друго на света478“, изследването задава въпроса дали е възможно да се позиционира напълно ЕС във вече съществуваща рамка от интеграционни модели или по-скоро би следвало да бъде направен опит да се потърси нова рамка за неговото развитие. 2. Обособяване на две нови измерения в интеграционното развитие на европейския проект – еволюционна и адаптивна интеграция: (cid:135)(cid:3) еволюционна интеграция, базираща се на уникалността и развитието на самия Съюз, съчетаващ както познати интеграционни елементи, така и такива, произтичащи от липсата на негов аналог; (cid:135)(cid:3) адаптивна интеграция, която е в резултат на определени събития, в които страните осъзнават неспособността си да се справят сами. В резултат, те констатират необходимостта от обща визия за ЕС и формират общи действия, определящи посоката на интеграционно развитие и устойчивост на европейския проект. Когато се развиват възможни сценарии за бъдещето на европейския проект и степента на неговата интеграция, един от най-съществените компоненти е „невидимият“, този свързан с ценностите, вярванията и мечтите, както на гражданите, така и на вземащите решение в ЕС. 3. Дефиниране на идея за осъзнаване хоризонталния характер на политиката за сигурност и преосмисляне процеса на бюджетно планиране в държавите-членки, включвайки елемента сигурност към бюджетните пера на различни секторни политики, извън вътрешен ред и сигурност и отбрана, а именно – енергетика, околна среда, икономика и финанси, транспорт, наука, образование, младеж, култура, здравеопазване, туризъм, селско стопанство, социална политика. Така сигурността ще залегне в стратегическите документи на различни секторни политики, водещи до осъзнаване и отразяване на нейния комплексен характер, като същевременно бюджетната тежест ще бъде по-балансирано разпределена; 4. Определяне на изводи, в контекста на темата на изследването, които могат да послужат в процеса на подготовка на България за председателството на Съвета на ЕС през 2018г. – да залегне компонентът сигурност в очертаващите се към момента приоритети за 2018г. – енергетика – енергийна сигурност; единен дигитален пазар – киберсигурност; миграционни потоци от юг и изток и стратегическа визия след 2020г. Допълнително анализът на председателствата, обхващащи темпоралния обхват на разработката от 2009-2013г., показва, че всяко от тях включва сред приоритетите си елемент, свързан с позиционирането на ЕС на международната сцена, което следва да се вземе предвид при сформирането на дневния ред на ЕС в рамките на бъдещето първо българско председателство; (cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3) 478 Уилям Сароян, „Нещо като нож, нещо като цвете, изобщо като нищо на света“ (cid:3) 320 5. Липсата към момента на актуална стратегия по въпросите на сигурността и отбраната в ЕС, поставя под въпрос неговото ниво на амбиции – какъв вид играч иска да бъде, какъв тип сила да използва твърда или мека, какво да е взаимодействието с НАТО, предвид, че двете организации работят на един театър на операции, какво е нивото на политическа зрялост в страните-членки и подкрепата на обществеността за развитието на ОПСО. Дефинирането на нивото на амбиция на ЕС, неговите стратегически цели и военни способности е от ключово значение за бъдещето позициониране на Европейския съюз в глобалното състезание. Усложнената ситуация в Близкия изток и Северна Африка не следва да бъде повод за поставяне под съмнение съществуването на ЕС и неговата същност като sui generis, уникален по своята същност съюз. В трудни моменти „съмненията в себе си“, в „собствените способности“ следва да мобилизират политическа воля и обединена стратегическа визия за адаптирането на ЕС към новите реалности, а не да водят до неговото подценяване и обезличаване. За разлика от много други играчи на международната сцена, ЕС е най-големият нетен износител на помощ за трети страни. ЕС бе награден с Нобеловата награда за мир за успеха си като мирен интеграционен проект. Самият факт, че бежанският поток днес е насочен именно към Европа, независимо от непосредствената близост на други държави, по-близки по своя цивилизационен характер до страните им на произход, доказва предимствата и постиженията на Европейския съюз. Силните страни на ЕС не следва да бъдат изтъквани като негова слабост – т.нар. „мека сила“. По-скоро дефицитът на определени способности следва да бъде компенсиран, а не да се омаловажава наличието на такива. За целта е необходима модернизация на Европейската стратегия за сигурност, която да притежава дизайна на интелигентна стратегия, отговаряща на новите реалности и предизвикателства в средата за сигурност. В тази връзка ЕС следва да бъде дефиниран като интелигентна сила, което означава съчетание от твърда и мека сила в ефективни (cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3) 479 Както бе подробно представено вече в текста, идеята на българското правителство (2009-2013) за Бяла книга за отбрана, се състои в създаването на платформа за европейски анализ на състоянието, предизвикателствата и изискванията към развитието на бъдещите способности на ЕС. (cid:3) 322 ABSTRACT EU SECURITY AND DEFENCE AFTER THE LISBON TREATY AND NATO’S STRATEGIC CONCEPT OF 2010 The current monograph is conducted in the period 2012–2015 and aims at describing and analyzing the “snapshot“ of EU security and defence after the Lisbon treaty and NATO’s strategic concept of 2010. The study has a temporal scope 2009-2013, but takes into account the developments in 2014– ’15 related to *EU elections and EC political will for a new foreign policy strategy and EU army; *The NATO Wales summit; *Complex developments in Ukraine, the Middle East and North Africa. I. GENERAL SCOPE 1. Topic and subject of analysis The topic of the current monograph is about the security and defence problems the European Union faces in the new security environment. Subject of the research is the cooperation between the EU and NATO in overcoming problems and new threats in the security environment, given that 22 out of 28 EU member states481 are also part of NATO. For the purposes of the study the Author constructs a theoretical model defining the security environment as an independent variable, the EU and NATO security and defence strategic papers as dependent variables. 2. Relevance Selecting EU Security and Defence after the Lisbon Treaty and NATO’s Strategic Concept of 2010 as the topic was suggested by geopolitical changes and lively debate on formulation and adoption of the 2010 NATO Strategic Concept and overall restructuring of EU Common Foreign Policy and Common Security and Defence Policy after the Lisbon Treaty. That the subject is relevant and topical is shown by: (cid:135)(cid:3) The potential of EU security and defence policy in the qualitatively new environment and legal framework after the 2009 Lisbon Treaty which reorganises EU Foreign Policy and Defence; (cid:135)(cid:3) NATO’s 2010 strategic reassessment and New Strategic Concept; (cid:135)(cid:3) Expectations of a new EU strategic vision from the December Council (the December 2013 European Council on Defence); (cid:135)(cid:3) The current security environment, global and regional risks and threats; (cid:135)(cid:3) The economic and financial crisis and defence budget cuts by EU members, 22 of which are also in NATO; (cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3) 481 EU before “Brexit” and activation of article 50 of Lisbon treaty according to which – any Member State may decide to withdraw from the Union in accordance with its own constitutional requirements. (cid:3) 323 (cid:135)(cid:3) The lack of recent updates to the 2003 EU Security strategy in ‘A Secure Europe in a Better World’, ESS, last amplified in 2008, after three EU enlargements brought eight new members, and six years after the Lisbon Treaty. The study makes recommendations482 which need endorsing and amplifying with potential EU security and defence visions after developments in 2014–’15: *EU elections and EC political will for a new foreign policy strategy and EU army; *The NATO Wales summit; *Complex developments in Ukraine, the Middle East and North Africa. The first two Chapters show the need to update the EU security strategy in order to meet security environment threats. Chapter Three looks at the road from strategic paper formulation to implementation, and: (cid:135)(cid:3) On the one hand tests the first two Chapters’ theses, hypotheses, conclusions and recommendations through a empirical survey involving an expert assessment questionnaire completed by 35 national and EU level respondents (politicians: ministers, parliamentarians, MEPs, commissioners, political advisers), the military, diplomats, and sectoral specialists conducted between March and May 2015; (cid:135)(cid:3) On the other, follows the new dynamics from the vantage of EU process symptoms to: (cid:16)(cid:3) Identify challenges emerging after the new EU Security Strategy, and (cid:16)(cid:3) Present, without claiming exhaustiveness, potential scenarios in the context of the Common Security and Defence Policy (CSDP). 3. Aims and tasks The main aim of the study is to present the challenges in the modern security environment calling for better EU and NATO cooperation in a new strategic context. Specific aims and tasks may be grouped as follows: From the current security environment point of view: (cid:135)(cid:3) A survey of EU policies in the qualitatively new environment and statutory framework after the 2009 Lisbon Treaty and the 2010 NATO Strategic Concept; (cid:135)(cid:3) An analysis of risks and complex threats in the security and defence environment; (cid:135)(cid:3) An analysis of the challenges to security and defence: *the impact of the economic and financial crisis on national and EU defence sector funding; *differing risk and threat perception both within the EU and across both sides of the Atlantic; *the need for greater trust and better information and particularly intelligence exchange between EU and NATO Allies; *the significance of energy security and global commons; *globalisation and deeper transparency in defence and democratic control over that sector; (cid:135)(cid:3) constructing a theoretical model revealing the causality between changes in the security environment and the EU and NATO strategic papers. From the point of view of EU/NATO cooperation: (cid:135)(cid:3) A study of EU/NATO cooperation and of initiatives on smart defence and capability pooling and sharing; (cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3) 482 Some of those recommendations were made by the Author in her capacity as MP at the plenary sessions of the 41st National Assembly of the Republic of Bulgaria (2009–2012) and its EU, foreign policy and defence committees, and as MEP (2012–2014) in the EP Security and Defence Subcommittee (see Annex 1). (cid:3) 324 (cid:135)(cid:3) An analysis of the challenges in front of and between the two organizations; (cid:135)(cid:3) An analysis of the events in Libya and Ukraine as EU and NATO challenges from the south and east in the context of the two organisations’ cooperation and role; (cid:135)(cid:3) An analysis of Bulgaria as a recent EU and NATO member with specific experience in southeast Europe and the Black Sea region, highlighting in practical terms: *the strategic rethinking process at the national level; *implementing both NATO smart defence and the EU’s pooling and sharing approach. From the point of view of formulating conclusions and potential scenarios for the Common Security and Defence Policy (CSDP): (cid:135)(cid:3) Formulating recommendations for developing and raising the degree of EU security and defence; (cid:135)(cid:3) Presenting potential scenarios for future CSDP development and its cooperation with NATO. 4. Thesis and Hypotheses The research thesis is as follows: EU security and defence requires a strategic rethink of the security environment and an update of the European Security Strategy. Proving the thesis involves the following three hypotheses: (cid:135)(cid:3) Hypothesis 1: The current security environment has changed; (cid:135)(cid:3) Hypothesis 2: There is causality between changes in the security environment and EU and NATO strategic papers; (cid:135)(cid:3) Hypothesis 3: The current security environment calls for improved cooperation between the EU and NATO. The research questions are: 1. What are the characteristics of contemporary security environment? 2. What is the causal relationship between the changes in the security environment, the EU and NATO strategic papers? 3. What ought a future EU security strategy to contain and which key factors/features should it to incorporate? 5. Methods and Approaches The study is not limited to mechanically collecting data and information on official papers and assessing them. It aims to analyse EU security and defence in a qualitatively new environment and statutory framework; to stress the uniqueness of the European Union; to obtain answers to the questions formulated within its set aims and tasks, and to highlight potential scenarios for CSDP development. This calls for applying an interdisciplinary approach plus diverse aspects of the analytical approach: retrospective, political theory, sociological, and comparative. A systematic approach is also used to comprehend the entities subject to examination and determine the extent to which the EU and NATO are capable of facing existing threats amid a more dynamic and diverse environment. Analysis and synthesis methods are used for primary and secondary information, generalisation, induction and deduction, in-depth interviews, and secondary data and survey analysis. (cid:3) 325 This contains an analysis of EU and NATO strategic papers and statutory instruments. The secondary data analysis uses public opinion and perception surveys483 and data comparing defence spending on both sides of the Atlantic484. A theoretical model which does not claim exhaustiveness is constructed to highlight the causal relationship between the security environment as an independent variable and the security and defence strategic papers emanated by the EU and NATO as agents through their bodies, structures and leaderships. The monograph contains a dedicated empirical study involving collecting and analysing sociological data, conducting in-depth interviews, and obtaining responses by 35 national and EU level respondents between March and May 2015 in five stages: *Drawing up an expert assessment questionnaire; *Identifying suitable respondents and convening an expert group; *Organising the expert assessment; *Conducting the expert assessment; *Analysing and presenting the results and formulating set recommendations and forecasts. Details of the study are shown in detail in Part 3.1 of the monograph. The decision to select predominantly respondents with political expertise (practicing politicians, cabinet advisers, civil service experts briefing ministers and parliamentarians for delegations and EU and NATO summits, and diplomats) reflects the collective political nature of the two entities. Directly or indirectly, tangentially or partially, both are political. Considering the respondents’ positions and functions their comments and remarks are not attributed. Conclusions and findings are the Author’s summaries with deference to respondents’ diverse opinions and do not commit respondents or the bodies they represent. The anonymity offered to respondents eliminated the risk of politically correct responses and promoted frank opinions based on personal perception and experience. 6. Constraints The first constraint is time scale. The timescale is delineated by three key junctures: *The 2009 Lisbon Treaty; *The 2010 NATO Concept; *The December 2013 EU Council on Defence. The study covers the period: 1. After 2009 when the EU acquired the status of a legal subject – a new element in the Lisbon Treaty485 of great significance for the external dimension of EU actions. The Treaty introduced innovations into EU foreign, security, and defence policy. Linking diverse elements of EU foreign policy like diplomacy, security, trade, development, humanitarian aid and international negotiations is an innovation giving the EU a clearer voice on the international stage; 2. After 2010: a year of NATO strategic rethinking and the New Concept. PRESENTATION CHAPTER ONE: A RETROSPECTION OF EU AND NATO SECURITY AND DEFENCE PRIOR TO THE LISBON TREATY; NOTIONS AND THEORETICAL MODEL (cid:3) 1.1. Historical development of cooperation in European defence after the end of the Second World War The monograph conducts an historical retrospection with the understanding that history shows not so much the past as the future. The analysis of European security and defence between the Second World War and the 2003 European Security Strategy highlights three major trend groups:*European security and defence integration; *NATO and EDC/EU cooperation; * Sensitivity on national sovereignty. The trends may be presented thus: First, defence integration entails: (cid:135)(cid:3) A vision based on 1950s’ ideas and initiatives by Jean Monnet and René Pleven and the concept of a supranational European Defence Community (EDC); (cid:135)(cid:3) Tendency to greater integration when threats are immediate; (cid:135)(cid:3) Striving to boost European security in reaction to growing bloc confrontation and the June 1950 Korean War leading to US pressure on western Europe to hasten West German remilitarisation; (cid:135)(cid:3) Striving to balance countries within the integration area and prevent one (especially West Germany) having military superiority over the rest through common authorities, political and military command, and budget; (cid:135)(cid:3) Transitioning from a strongly federalist idea of European armed forces to gradual step- by- step defence integration; (cid:135)(cid:3) Elaborating integration stages as NATO membership followed by EU membership; (cid:135)(cid:3) Linking military and political integration as exemplified by the parallel launch of the European Defence Community and European Political Community concepts in 1952; (cid:135)(cid:3) The need for a single voice on international problems as exemplified by the Davignon Report; (cid:135)(cid:3) Reactivity, with events defining integration dynamics and national amenity to steps towards security and defence integration. This trend is typified by the answer British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan (1957–1963) famously gave a journalistic question about the hardest part of his work:”Events, dear boy, events!”488 The theoretical model reviews events and security environment changes capable of modifying the political and geopolitical landscape and occasioning set strategic actions. (cid:16)(cid:3) The 9/11 terrorist attacks on New York and Washington prompting adoption of the European Capabilities Action Plan (ECAP); the Iraq War prompting adoption of the Secure Europe in A Secure Europe in a Better World European Security Strategy. Second, trends in NATO/EDC/EU cooperation include: (cid:135)(cid:3) Reiterating the need to interact with NATO at each development stage of the European army concept; (cid:135)(cid:3) Even attempts to emancipate the EU in its own defence bear the mark of difficult implementation, as witnessed by the attempt at WEU independence and distancing from NATO. Many reasons for this trend emerged with the Maastricht concept and obtain to date: *defence clauses perceived differently by different member state nationals; *most EU members are also NATO members; * individual countries have conflicting views on whether the supranational approach or intergovernmental agreements should lead security and defence; (cid:135)(cid:3) The requirement for the EU’s voice to be heard in international relations is stressed alongside the duties nations assume within NATO. Third, sensitivity to sovereignty entails: (cid:135)(cid:3) Highlighting historical events and decisions showing readiness to cede national sovereignty in set historical junctures; (cid:135)(cid:3) British preference to remain aloof from EDC/EU integration; (cid:135)(cid:3) National parliament involvement in defence and the French parliament’s refusal to ratify the European Defence Community treaty due to unwillingness to participate in structures and mechanisms limiting national sovereignty; (cid:135)(cid:3) Major debate principles: supranational integration versus cooperation between sovereign states; (cid:135)(cid:3) Restricting the defence powers of supranational EU authorities (the European Parliament, the European Commission) in favour of ones exemplifying the intergovernmental principle in European integration (The European Council; the Council of the European Union). These past trends continue influencing the present. The Lisbon Treaty provides tools, but their use depends on political decisions and the will to greater security and defence integration. This calls for updating the European Security Strategy with a strategic reassessment of the security environment and a clear definition of the level of EU ambition in common foreign policy and security and defence policy. As key components of the study, both papers are reviewed in detail in a subsequent item reviewing EU security and defence. 1.2. Theoretical Model This part of the study postulates a theoretical model to generate arguments and examples confirming the Author’s hypothesis of a causal link between the security environment and relevant EU strategic papers. The Author also proves the hypothesis that today’s security environment has changed and presents the complex character of threats and the new strategic context in which agents have to operate. After defining the monograph’ main postulates, the theoretical model defines the security environment as an independent variable and strategic papers on security and defence by agents EU and NATO as a dependent variable. New global threats, challenges and insecurity in a much more interdependent world and concrete realities in immediate geographical proximity to the EU borders are stated as requiring to be taken into consideration in a single strategic paper if Europe wishes to play a key role in formulating the future global order. This in turn leads to the need to rethink the EU Security Strategy. The level of EU ambitions determines whether such a rethink shall produce an update to the current Strategy, or launch a new EU security and defence strategy or new EU global strategy. The Author attempts to present potential forward-looking solutions. Applying the proposals could potentially lead to a future theoretical model, but it’s needed a considerable time to spread awareness and to mobilize national and supranational resources and will. In brief, the three analysis steps relate to the historical part of the study which shows EU reactivity to security environment changes and events. Step one analyses the Cold War: a bipolar model with a clearly defined adversary and more predictable security environment. The agents react to the environment, but also shape it by emanating strategic papers. If the Cold War system was bipolar, stable, with clear adversaries and low probability of erroneous perception, today it is highly diffuse, with complex threats, and diverse national security environment perceptions and assessments. Step two analyses the theoretical model from the Cold War to date, featuring reactivity and a one- way influence from the new security environment to agents EU and NATO operating in a new system of international relations featuring a high degree of uncertainty. Figure 1: A theoretical model from the Cold War to date (cid:3) Source: the Author (cid:3) 331 The European Security Strategy is a case in point. Signing A Secure Europe in a Better World in 2003, Javier Solana and many other pro-Europeans wished to unite Europe behind a common strategic initiative after division over the US and Britain-led Iraq invasion489. Additional reasons included the growing scope of non-state organisations, mutual infrastructural connectedness leading to dependence and vulnerability, poverty and sickness leading to high mortality, the contest for natural resources and energy dependency. Step three analyses a potential future model in case a great part of the Author’s proposals for a future EU smart security490 and defence strategy combining soft and hard power and balancing strategic vision and flexibility were adopted. The EU would thus rise to new realities, anticipate, and act proactively rather than merely reacting to security environment changes. Figure 2: A potential future theoretical model (cid:3) Source: the Author This is an attempt to define the EU as a smart power formulating smart strategies entailing combination of soft and hard power and balance between strategic vision and flexibility. On the one hand, frequent risks of diverse form and intensity impact the agents and their authorities, forcing not only to react efficiently, but also to change effectively; i.e., by timely and effective action. On the other hand, the EU ought to be proactive and transform into a smart power; i.e. to harness soft and hard power in effective strategies. This vision supposes that a future EU security strategy would formulate a strategic vision for developing capabilities and positioning the EU on the world stage in a flexible manner taking account of unforeseen security environment developments. Proceeding from the understanding that states still have a legitimate monopoly on power in the field of security and defence, it ought to be noted that a balance is needed between liberal states and societies which integrate to an ever higher degree, share common aims and strive for eternal peace, and surrounding states and non-state actors which still reason in realist and neorealist frames. Cases in point are the Ukraine events and the annexation of the Crimea, and the rise of Islamic State in the Middle East. The focus of analysis is the CSDP viewed through the prisms of realism, neorealism, neoliberalism, to an extent constructivism, and the theory of macro level interdependence, in an attempt to explain EU cooperation. At the micro level, the CSDP is viewed through the prisms of rational choice and coalitions as regards relevant political decision making and the practical aspects of cooperation. The Lisbon treaty and the NATO strategic Concept in the context of european security and defence The Lisbon Treaty ushered important changes to ESDP/CSDP aiming to boost the EU’s role and tools in areas like crisis management, human rights and international development, and inject consistency into foreign policy through improving coordination: introducing a EU High Representative for foreign policy and security and a EU Council Chair, and launching the European External Action Service. Specific changes open CSDP opportunities to deepen defence cooperation and boost the EU’s significance as a factor in international security. The Treaty mentions the European Defence Agency for the first time; broadens the scope of CSDP missions (Petersberg Tasks); introduces solidarity and common defence clauses and the Permanent Structured Cooperation mechanism. Despite these improvements, the level of EU ambitions as a defensive community remains unclear. Thus, the common defence clause (Article 42.7) foresees help to any member state subject to armed attack on its soil, yet does not specify whether this includes armed means. While reminiscent of Atlantic Treaty Article 5, the clause requires interpretation in practice. The Lisbon Treaty does not set a clear CSDP EU homeland defensive task. All references to defence and operational planning relate to operations outside the EU. This significantly curtails command system and military organisation options within the EU. Alongside a shortage of key military capabilities for external operations, the EU faces serious difficulties in organising the command structure for each operation because appointing operational commanders and staffs, as well as force commanders and staffs in operational areas, does not rely on an existing command system, as in NATO, but on activating operational staffs and personnel offered by member states. The 200-odd-strong International EU International Military Staff (some 5 percent of the EU External Action Service) does not allow strategic rapid planning in addition; reinforcements from member states are foreseen in crises. By comparison, the NATO International Military Staff is many times larger and can plan all operations independently. The inclusion of the CSDP into the December 2013 Council agenda for the first time after the Lisbon Treaty is an advance showing heads of state’s definite political commitment to security and defence. Their decisions formed the following three CSDP clusters: *Effectiveness, visibility, and influence; *Boosting capability creation; *Strengthening the European defence industry. These clusters ought to form a roadmap to more specific plans for CSDP development and optimum coordination with NATO. The task set by the Council to the High Representative in coordination with member states – to assess the influence of changes to the global security environment and define challenges before the EU by 2015 – offers a good opportunity to update the 2003 EU Security Strategy or formulate a new one in line with current realities. Alongside defining strategic interest, the EU ought to review its capabilities and develop a new 2020-2025 capability plan. The Agency’s 45 main remit is raising member state military capabilities by: (cid:120)(cid:3)Defining common member state capability aims; (cid:120)(cid:3)Launching and implementing programmes to attain set aims; Harmonising member state operational needs as a way of improving weapon supplies; Managing defence technology R&D; (cid:120)(cid:3)Contributing to boosting the European Defence Technological and Industrial Base, including boosting the efficiency of defence spending. Article 42.6, Permanent Structured Closer defence cooperation between some member 46 Protocol Cooperatio n – a new states. Permanent Structured Cooperation commits 10 on element (PESCO) members to more intensive defence capability Permanent development and offering armed combat units for Structured planned missions. The EDA regularly assesses Cooperation participating member state contributions. under TEU The Council adopts Permanent Structured Cooperation Article 42 by qualified majority at the request of member states. There is no restriction on inviting states, each of which may continue Permanent Structured Cooperation so long as it fulfils commitments, or end it. The membership of new countries or the suspension of some of them is decided by the Council and depends on the level of fulfillment of their commitments. The NATO 2010 Strategic Concept attempts in its turn to answer both types of threat adequately: asymmetric global and regional threats and internal ones relating to territorial and public defence and new components noted by the World Economic Forum: economic, financial, energy, environmental, social, and justice. The following key aspects of the NATO Concept repay attention in the context of this study: First: the Alliance shall continue discharging three vital main tasks, each contributing to the security of member nations in accord with international law: collective defence, crisis management, and cooperative security. (cid:3) 336 Second: NATO shall continue being a unique and main forum for consultation on all matters affecting members’ territorial integrity and political independence according to Washington Treaty Article 4. Third: while the Alliance shall not consider any state its adversary, nobody should doubt its determination where the security of any member nation might be in jeopardy495. The NATO Concept aims at strategic balance between Washington Treaty Article 5 operations and those outside its scope; an active political role in energy security; continuing the open doors course and stressing public diplomacy as a key factor for successful implementation of security policy through better public awareness and overcoming stereotypes. (cid:3) CHAPTER TWO: AN ANALYSIS OF EU AND NATO COOPERATION This Chapter directs attention to the hypothesis that today’s security environment calls for better EU/NATO cooperation. After presenting the main aspects of the cooperation framework, the development of relations between the two entities, and their cooperation in post- conflict recovery and overcoming crises, the Author analyses challenges facing the EU and NATO from three angles: - Economic and financial: the financial crisis’ impact on defence budgets; European defence funding and science and technology investment; the future of the fragmented and uncompetitive European defence industry caused by its multiple separated national military-industrial complexes and national markets. Given that each country has armed forces facing new threats and budgetary restrictions, achieving coordination and cooperation by European Alliance members is seen to call for synergy between NATO smart defence projects and EU pooling and sharing initiatives. The Author also propounds the idea of a European defence semester similar to that in new EU economic governance, to be coordinated by the European Defence Agency; - Political: hindrances to EU/NATO cooperation in the context of: Cypriot/Turkish relations; differing risk and threat perceptions either side of the Atlantic; political dependence on public confidence and the effect of new media on formulating security environment actions and attitudes; - Institutional: the need to improve information exchange, particularly in intelligence, and the importance of security and defence parliamentary control. This stresses the significance of the Berlin Plus agreement between the two entities and recommends applying it to improve Turkey/EU and Cyprus/NATO relations by involving Ankara in the European Defence Agency and involving Cyprus fully into Partnership for Peace (PfP). The above proves the hypotheses that the EU and NATO need to interact better and that there is a causal connection between security environment developments and EU and NATO strategic papers. Examples include: *The economic and financial crisis leading to NATO’s 2010 New Strategic Concept launching the idea of smart defence, and the EU Pooling and Sharing Mechanism; *The launch of the European Energy Security Strategy after geopolitical developments and in recognition of EU dependence on energy commodity imports. Analysing NATO and EU cooperation sets off from the five criteria formulated by P Cornish: (cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3) 495 Strategic Concept for the Defence and Security of the Members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation adopted by Heads of State and Government in Lisbon, Active Engagement, Modern Defence <http://www. nato.int/lisbon2010/strategic- concept-2010-eng.pdf> (cid:3) 337 *geopolitical burden sharing by territory and role; *operational cooperation: Berlin Plus and beyond; *rapid reaction force planning: NATO response forces and EU Battlegroups units; *resource and capability planning; *responses to terrorism496. (cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3) 496 Cornish, P, “EU and NATO: Co-operation or Competition?,” Briefing paper, European Parliament, Directorate-General External Policies, October, 2006. <http://www.europarl.europa.eu/meetdocs/2004_2009/ papers/dv/eunatorelations_/eunatorelations_en.pdf> (cid:3) (cid:3) 338 (cid:16)(cid:3)Differing European perceptions of Russia, its policy of balancing power, and defensiveness against potential NATO eastern expansion, lend promise into the idea of reversing the integration stage sequence. This involves post-Soviet republics joining the EU first and NATO after. Russian relations with NATO are military-political, while mutual economic dependence and the lack of geopolitical competition between the EU and Russia offer a good basis for dialogue and mutually acceptable solutions. Moscow’s efforts to retain influence in the post-Soviet economic and political area are not likely to subside, and it is more important for Europe’s future to expand its economic area eastward rather than expand the Euro-Atlantic area there. NATO expansion can focus on the Western Balkans as a priority and the EU can intensify its Eastern Partnership. Whether the EU becomes a factor for resolving rather than deepening problems will depend on the strategic approach it chooses. The diverse combinations of strategies, tactics and techniques contain a principled negotiation method developed by a Harvard project497 and also termed benefits- based negotiation. It is an alternative to positional negotiation and could be of value if applied by the EU and Russia in the current circumstances. Principled negotiation involves distancing people from problems, concentrating on interests rather than positions, elaborating a multitude of possibilities before deciding on actions, and making each solution rest on an objective standard. Principled negotiation strategy combines elements of hard and soft power. Benefits- based negotiation means making Russia realise the need to cooperate with the EU and partner NATO strategically given no better optimum long term alternative. (the so called BATNA-best alternative of the negotiated agreement). Practice shows that refusal to take account of realities leads to all participants lagging in the global contest. The greater the desire and will to cooperate, the more methods stimulating agreement, cooperation and confidence weigh by comparison to confrontational ones. Optimum use of situational factors is of key importance, enabling the parties to enact their agendas, interpretations and solutions to the utmost498. In the above context, paraphrasing Strobe Talbott’s words that countries would define their “strength – indeed, … very greatness – not in terms of … ability to achieve or maintain dominance over others, but in terms of … ability to work with others in the interest of the international community as a whole,“499 it should be noted that the sole way to avoid a zero-sum outcome is not to allow strategic partnership evaluating in potential cold cooperation to transform in new Cold War with Russia. (cid:3) (cid:3) 347 (cid:3) (cid:3) 3.2 Potential EU security and defence scenarios This part of the study notes that even if a new EU security and defence strategy were adopted, it doesn’t guarantee its automatic implementation. The two key challenges here are related: *on the one hand, with how well the strategy paper responds to the key aspects elaborated in the monograph’ Chapters One and Two: (cid:135)(cid:3) A clear definition of the level of EU ambitions; (cid:135)(cid:3) A review of EU foreign policy and security and defence policy tools, plus relating security policy to development, good neighbourly relations and enlargement. The focus should be on the EU’s major tools of development aid, trade, humanitarian aid, crisis reaction, and taking part in international operations; (cid:135)(cid:3) Defining EU/NATO relations, resolving the Cyprus question, the need for an intensive intelligence exchange; applying the Berlin Plus agreements; (cid:135)(cid:3) Launching a European defence semester by analogy to the one in new EU economic governance and reviewing the European Defence Agency’s potential coordinating role in defence budgeting; (cid:135)(cid:3) Compiling a white paper inventorying EU capabilities, to be followed by an action plan on modernising and optimising capabilities to a level adequate to current dynamics; (cid:135)(cid:3) Deciding whether the Lisbon Treaty Article 42.7 is an analogue of NATO Article 5 or affords other interpretations; (cid:135)(cid:3) Reviewing the role of parliamentary control at the national and European levels; (cid:135)(cid:3) Reviewing the role of communications strategies in generating public backing for the security and defence sector; (cid:3) 348 (cid:135)(cid:3) Permanent structured cooperation, differentiation: necessity or opportunity?; (cid:135)(cid:3) Deploying Battlegroups; (cid:135)(cid:3) The Eastern Partnership – the Western Balkans, what shall be the EU expansion priorities; (cid:135)(cid:3) The place of neutral nations (Austria, Sweden, Finland, Ireland and Switzerland), the two EU members other than Austria, Sweden, Finland and Ireland which are not in NATO (Cyprus and Malta) and Denmark, whose special status, the 1992 referendum and the National Compromise make it participate partially in four European integration areas, in particular common foreign and security policy and common defence policy; (cid:135)(cid:3) Emerging threats directly related to EU, rather than trans-Atlantic security (immigration and refugee waves into the Old Continent from North Africa and the Middle East; the appearance of European-born foreign fighters); (cid:135)(cid:3) An analysis of fundamental factors like possible integration stages, global security and perceptions of it, institutional limitations and EU and NATO decision making; (cid:135)(cid:3) The thrust to new technologies in the European defence industry; (cid:135)(cid:3) Generating unified perceptions of risk and threat in individual member states. *On the other hand, with spanning the compilation of a strategic paper and its implementation, bearing in mind the great risk of the paper being declarative and lacking a clear strategic vision, and/or of its encompassing too broad a range of issues and spheres given the complex nature of challenges, thus losing the clear definition of priorities. Five sets of challenges emerge: First, insufficient political will and confidence within the EU in the context of 22 of the 28 being in NATO, and insufficient consensus between EU members in prioritising threats and challenges. Strategic differences between EU members reflecting geography, traditional partnerships and historical threats make consensus difficult. The lack of sufficient political will is a challenge before CSDP development, manifest both in the use of armed force by the EU and boosting the positions of common structures and organisations. Specific examples include unused EU Battlegroups and the still-uncertain position of the European Defence Agency. The level of trust between member states in turn makes CSDP implementation difficult. Initiatives like pooling and sharing assume high mutual dependence and can thus be implemented only amid high confidence and no concerns about sharing capabilities, especially classified information and intelligence. Lack of confidence also hampers cooperation with NATO and the practical use of the Berlin Plus mechanism for EU access to Alliance capabilities. It is also critical in resolving the issue between Cyprus and Turkey. The need for greater EU political and military integration, particularly in the context of recent events in North Africa, the Middle East, and Ukraine, is palpable and calls for political will and confidence. The second set of challenges is the fragmentation of defensive capability and the lack of a united vision on complementarity and an integrated approach. The level of EU ambition ought to rise to end reliance that the US and NATO will provide the major input for Euro-Atlantic defence. The lessons of past and current EU operations show lacking or insufficient key capabilities like strategic airlift, aerial refueling, intelligence and surveillance. Creating these expensive capabilities is beyond a single nation and calls for boosting cooperation between EU members. They ought to assess positively the Council’s commitment to creating critical capabilities and make up the critical shortfall of (cid:3) 349 capabilities through specific European Defence Agency projects like Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems (RPAS), Air-to-Air Refuelling Capacity, Satellite Communication, and Cyber. The classical understanding of defence should change amid blurring boundaries between internal and foreign security and the EU has to acquire the ability to defend its strategic interests globally, otherwise there is a risk to turn into an anaemic regionally bound actor. The third set of challenges concerns the worrying trend to EU defence spending cuts, partly because of the world economic and financial crisis and partly because of the propensity, especially within the Eurozone, to cutting the defence share of national budgets (under 1.3 percent of GDP). Europe spends half of the US budget on defence. On average, half of EU members’ spend covers personnel, 30 percent cover operations and maintenance, and 20 percent on supplies. Combat system and capability fragmentation means that the biggest share of arms spending is at national level. At the same time, countries like Russia, China and India are boosting military spending significantly. The fourth set of challenges is a natural extension of the third and relates to European and US public and decision maker perceptions of CSDP import and added value. After two world wars in the 20th Century, Europeans instinctively reject armed conflict in resolving problems. Asked if war is possible and fair in imposing justice, just 28 percent of the EU public and 45 percent of EU politicians answer positively, compared to over 75 percent of the US public and politicians. The conclusion is that Europe follows the logic of peace versus the US “logic of war”501. The fifth set of challenges affects both countries and the international community and comprises four trends: “new wars” or domestic conflicts that significantly threaten regional and international security; growing numbers of victims of domestic crises and conflicts, mass migration and international crises; the international community’s unpreparedness for effective intervention in domestic conflicts due to the fine line between non-interference in sovereign affairs and objectively justified defence of human rights; the emergence of post-Cold War “weak states” marked by instability, overlapping authorities, and domestic conflicts stemming amid collapsing authority and failed states502. The three important formulas retain significance after adoption of a new strategic paper, viz.: (cid:135)(cid:3) The formula of power expressed through an objective analysis of resources available to the EU, its desire and its political will to employ them and skill to use them. (cid:135)(cid:3) The sustainable decision formula: *intellectual imagination linked to clear strategic (cid:135)(cid:3) vision;*political will to translate words into clear action plans, and *public support both for the financial dimensions of Common foreign policy and Common Security and Defence Policy, and for EU participation in missions of its own, alongside NATO, or internationally. (cid:135)(cid:3) The movement formula, including the components of direction, speed, and time, with the understanding that development is “forward movement”. The direction formula contains the speed and time components. Amid globalisation, they are key to the adequacy, competitiveness, effectiveness and efficiency of individual, national, or supranational entities. Recent events in the Middle East, North Africa and Ukraine show ever more clearly the need for a strategic vision that takes into account both the new dynamics and the new realities in European security and defence. The emergence of a new impetus in 2015 highlighted certain symptoms in EU processes: on the one hand: they tend to be reactive rather than proactive in certain situations, on the other hand the EU (cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3) 501 German Marshall Fund and Compagnia di San Paolo, Transatlantic Trends: Leaders, 2011 <http://trends. gmfus.org/> 502 Гочев, А., „Конфликтът. Теории и подходи за разрешаване“, „Албатрос“, Sofia, 2011 [Gochev, A, Conflict: Theories and Approaches to Solutions] (cid:3) 350 authorities’ terms of reference play a role. The facts that it was the new European Commission that launched the new vision, and that the process began after the Ukraine crisis and the MENA503 refugee flows from Morocco to Iran showed that the eventual paper would hardly be innovative. It would rather be expected to be adaptive, confirming the findings of the theoretical model. Forming a strategic vision based not on transient influence but on analysing and anticipating events to curb their potential negative effects would give the EU a competitive advantage. An innovative strategy involves anticipating problems, managing processes (through very good internal coordination) before final decisions, shaping approaches and instruments adequate to new realities, threats and risks facing EU security and defence. The EU ought to overcome one of its basic internal challenges, namely action – whose absence or delay render it equal to inaction. The actions of member states and European authorities need to be synchronised, balanced, and underwritten by political will to identify problems in time, analyse them in depth, articulate them comprehensively to the public, and resolve them adequately. Leaving the formation of a set strategic vision for the new EC after the 2014 European Parliament elections has a certain political logic to do with the configuration of the new EP as regards the predomination of pro-European parties or parties opposed to deepening European integration, the EC agenda and the priorities of its chair, appointed for the first time after a contest between European party nominees. In short, a political logic to do with overall political will and vision for “more” or “less” Europe. Looking, however, at the processes and challenges to security, this awaiting approach of reacting to problems after they appear, is more of a handicap than an advantage. Strategic cycles are traditionally longer than political ones precisely so that short-term fluctuations do not affect them. The December 2013 Council found only that “defence matters” and then the entire first half of 2014 European authorities’ energies went into an election campaign, the administration in turn awaiting developments until the new political leadership began functioning only in late 2014. Time is the sole irreplaceable resource and failing to use it, amid globalisation, instability at Europe’s borders, and asymmetric threats to security, can find little justification. These symptoms may also be regarded in the contest of integration processes. One very often sees debates on the direction the EU ought to take: a union of sovereign nations, a federation, or a confederation. This study also features an attempt to find arguments in favour of the federal option, particularly as regards European security. Following the logic, however, that the EU model is unique and so far unprecedented, one may attempt to regard its integration in a different way. When regarding an unprecedented sui generis organisation, we may ask whether the EU can position itself within an existing integration model or whether it ought to seek a new framework of its development. Defining such a framework remains in the realm the so called “invisible art” in which a blank sheet of paper invites observers to mobilise their imagination and depict or write their own creations or scenarios. Chancellor Adenauer said that at the beginning European Union was the dream of a few that grew into a hope for the many and into a necessity for all. With time, three key aspects of European project development emerge: (cid:135)(cid:3) Integration at different speeds, reflecting the degree of individual countries’ willingness to surrender sovereignty in set areas. This may conditionally be termed lowest common integration denominator; (cid:135)(cid:3) Integration following set events leading to new challenges and changing the situation. This may conditionally be termed adaptive integration; (cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3) 503 MENA – The Middle East and North Africa (cid:3) 351 (cid:135)(cid:3) Staged integration that automatically doesn’t make EU accession equal to EU integration. (cid:135)(cid:3) This integration is a process of continually offering proof and readiness for ever closer integration into the likes of the Schengen Agreement, the Eurozone, or Banking Union. The above reasoning allows an attempt to plot new aspects of integration on the “ blank sheet”, without excluding other interpretations: First, from the viewpoint of the EU’s uniqueness, evolutionary integration resting on intrinsic development combining known integration elements and ones stemming from the lack of an analogy. Borrowing from William Saroyan, we may define the EU as “knife-like, flower-like, like nothing at all in the world“: international organisation-like, federation-like, like nothing else in the world. Second, from the viewpoint of adaptive integration that follows challenges individual nations cannot handle alone, driving them to acknowledge shared visions and clear plans for European project sustainability. Advancing in “invisible art”, we could make a link with a message from de Saint-Exupéry’s Little Prince: “what is essential is invisible to the eye“. Here, we note that when developing potential future European integration scenarios, one of the most significant components is indeed the invisible one to do with values, beliefs and aspirations of both the public and EU decision makers. When values are shared, they can form the backbone of an organisation (like the EU) or partnership (like the Euro-Atlantic one) and a legitimate basis for policy. Given the topic of this monograph, the above in turn evolves scenarios for EU security and defence. Three potential scenarios, in addition to the one currently obtaining, emerge in the context of EU security and defence: 1. The EU optimising its capabilities within the framework of NATO. The EU’s role within the Alliance entails three main points: (cid:135)(cid:3) Developing criteria to help decisions as to which crises the EU has a leading role in bearing in mind its definition of a “soft power.” (cid:135)(cid:3) European countries in NATO and the EU ought to have a clearly structured mechanism for cooperation and intelligence exchange within Europe or for joint operations by both organisations, enabling rapid and adequate reaction, optimum resource use, a high degree of complementarity between countries, and a shared vision about the desired outcome and the manner of pursuing it. (cid:135)(cid:3) NATO and the EU ought to create a new framework for consultations and cooperation as regards the non-military aspects of security since the experience of the Balkans, Afghanistan and Iraq shows that military advance is difficult without a civil strategy. Though 22 of 28 NATO allies are European, the approach and assumption of commitments by decision makers differs because of the two organisations’ different formats. A way to overcoming this is to make NATO a two pillar organisation: the EU plus Norway, Iceland, Turkey, Albania, and the USA and Canada. This idea ought, however, to take into account the fact that NATO guarantees its members’ security and not in any way that of non-members, leaving open the question of Cyprus, Malta and neutral Austria, Sweden, Finland, Ireland, and Switzerland. This option does not exclude cooperating with NATO to the principle of smart defence. It also reflects current trends in other integration policies for the staged accession by EU members to more internal integration spaces like the Eurozone, Schengen and Banking Union. The scenario entails both closer convergence between member states in defence and boosting the striving to catch up by member states lagging in modernising their military capabilities. The likelihood of this scenario’s implementation is greatest since it has a ready legal instrument and possibilities laid on in the Lisbon Treaty, itself a step ahead in EU integration that is accepted and that unites all member states. It is work recalling that the Lisbon Treaty was needed to allow the EU to cope with the complex nature of 21st Century threats and deploy its full potential. Among the Treaty’s main aims was precisely to make the EU more effective and capable in tackling today’s world challenges: climate change, security, and sustainable development505. In this scenario NATO continues playing a key role in Old Continent security and defence, yet with a much greater commitment and striving for capability building by the European Allies. 3. Independent European armed forces, viewed through the prism of deepening European integration, raising the effectiveness of European foreign policy and the EU’s image on the international scene, as well as optimising the EU’s capabilities by supplementing NATO rather than duplicating it. Allowing the EU to be independent and enter the ultimate integration stage calls for two factors: system independence and balance. To this end, the EU ought to have European army and identity, and to occupy a clearly defined position within NATO. Currently, though EU NATO members spend some euro 195 billion a year on defence, or twice as much as Russia and more than China spends officially, the general perception is that EU security and defence are guaranteed by NATO, with a strong stress on US help. The expert analysis assesses the two likeliest possibilities on the basis of replies to the question when European army might appear as either in ten years’ time (28 percent) or never (27 percent). The main opinions voiced by respondents are as follows: (cid:135)(cid:3) Raising European army is a staged process involving broad public debate, formal legislation, and establishment of armed forces. Any stage can change through the direct impact of external factors, most importantly on the security environment; (cid:135)(cid:3) A European army would offer significant economies; (cid:135)(cid:3) Integration in defence(cid:3)area is possible since conditions call for it; (cid:135)(cid:3) Raising European army would inevitably move at uneven speeds and would involve geometric warping; (cid:135)(cid:3) A European army in the sense of a common classical set of forces is barely imaginable because of political, military, economic, cultural, and legal peculiarities in member states; (cid:135)(cid:3) National sovereignty will always outweigh collective security management. The two key issues facing the idea of a European army are: (cid:16)(cid:3)Whether it would be similar to NATO, i.e. without a single command, but rather depend on member state armed forces while setting Alliance-type defence budget indicators, personnel spend, and maintenance and investment spend (NATO: 2 percent of GDP; 50:25:25); (cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3) 505 „Лисабонският договор – ефективност, демокрация, прозрачност“, Представителство на Европейската комисия в България, София, 2008 <http://ec.europa.eu/bulgaria/papers/citizens/online_publications/lisbon_treaty.pdf> [The Lisbon Treaty: Effectiveness, Democracy, Transparency] (cid:3) 354 (cid:16)(cid:3)Or whether it will follow the supranational European Defence Community (EDC) vision with *common command; *common armed forces in identical uniform, a common training system, uniform weaponry and *a common budget, with exclusively defensive functions, deployed on member states’ soil. Each of the three scenarios has a certain degree of credibility, with the one envisaging permanent structured cooperation leading, followed by the one envisaging the EU if not as a second NATO pillar, at least with significantly boosted role as an alliance within the North Atlantic Treaty. Third comes the European army scenario. The third scenario has potential and federalist logic, but at the same time – many unknowns: First: on the one hand, we have European level political will expressed by the EC Chair. On the other hand, the key role for implementing the idea falls to member states. In view of the decision making mechanism and Britain’s categorical opposition, as well as likely similar positions by other members, the risk of repeating the fates of the Pleven plan and of the European Defence Community is too great. This is the place to recall that the United Kingdom has set a referendum on EU membership before 2017. Second: EU Defence suppliers appear to be active supporters of European army. Though this appears in concert with the logic of integration so far – that it rests on economic interests – it carries two risks: (cid:135)(cid:3) The temptation to create new capabilities and standards incompatible with Alliance ones. In this connection, it is important to apply standardisation and harmonisation patterns dovetailing with NATO ones, since 22 EU members are also NATO members, each with its own armed forces and defence budget. Applying smart defence principles, pooling and sharing resource and capability are followed by strategic partnership, cooperation and complementary. A powerful strategic partnership between NATO and the EU would add value both politically and operationally; (cid:135)(cid:3) The emergence of sizeable integration gaps between defence leader countries and countries with catching up economies. Third: Without a clear strategic vision defined in a new or updated European security strategy, it would be hard to assess the level of EU ambitions and the EU’s striving for a future positioning on the international stage. In turn, this calls to elaborate additional public arguments on the need for a European army. European leaders ought to be able to define their national viewpoints through the value it adds to common defensive potential, alongside sharing common strategic priorities formed through consistency and information exchange. A number of researchers define 2014 as a key juncture in redefining post-Cold War European security. The strategic landscape of European neighbourhood policy is radically changed. The two strategic surprises for Europe are: 1. Russia’s hybrid campaign along the eastern borders of the EU and NATO, and 2. the appearance of Middle East and North Africa (MENA) extremist groupings playing a key role in destabilising the entire Euro-Atlantic region and the unprecedented transformation of a terrorist movement into a quasi-state (Islamic State) threatening to disperse jihad through Europe506. Challenges in the Middle East and North Africa are entirely different from those in the East. The South set three great challenges before European security: (cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3) 506 Šedivý, J, Ambassador, “New unrest and instability on Europe’s periphery”, The European – Security and Defence Union, Edition 1, Volume 20, Brussels, 2015 <http://www.magazine-the-european.com> (cid:3) 355 1. The emergence of foreign fighters of European origin, religiously radicalised and ready to return to Europe and seek revenge through jihad. Terrorism in Europe appears where geopolitical circumstances intertwine with social issues like failed integration and radicalisation507. 2. The logic in elaborating CSDP development scenarios depends on the direction of EU development and particularly that of its security policy, and on the future cooperation with NATO. Here, the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation is taken as an extant and constant component playing a set role in diverse EU security and defence scenarios. The approach might, however, be different, were EU security and defence development to be defined by potential NATO development scenarios. In this regard, two scenarios elaborated by Stephan de Spiegeleire and Rem Korteweg for a study by the Clingendael Centre for Strategic Studies are reviewed. The main features they ascribe the North Atlantic Treaty are: *The transatlantic nexus: a sustainable political and operational connection between the American and European Allies; *US leadership: the scope of US participation in NATO and US desire to play a leading role; *Operational area: the geographical scope for NATO operations. *Decision making: the Alliance’s ability to settle disputes; *Top-down leadership: the degree to which NATO as an organisation can impose decisions and actions on its members; *Mission scope: the range within which NATO undertakes missions encompassing the entire conflict spectrum; *Capabilities: all available Alliance abilities and its efficiency in imposing them jointly; *Political as opposed to military essence: the balance between Alliance political and military dimensions. *Membership: broadening NATO’s geography with new members. Alongside this, they note three key factors that could change the above features: (cid:135)(cid:3) The will of the USA to lead NATO: strong US leadership or complete absence; (cid:135)(cid:3) EU influence: will the EU be a consistent political factor with the relevant weight in international politics (including in security), or will it be fragmented and hence weak; (cid:135)(cid:3) Threat perception: regardless of their nature, would the Allies perceive them as coming in 2025, or would divergent perceptions increase? There are five scenarios for the Alliance’s future according to them: (cid:16)(cid:3)NATO as an “efficient machine”, involving a strong US leadership, undisputed common vision on security and a relatively dispersed and weak Europe, since only a handful of European countries have the resource to operate alongside the US in the higher spectrum of combat. (cid:16)(cid:3)NATO as a “mutual partnership”, involving a combination of strong US leadership, a united and powerful Europe and a common perception of threats. (cid:16)(cid:3)NATO as a “dismantled machine”, involving an unwilling US leadership, a none-too- united Europe, and entirely divergent perception of threats. (cid:16)(cid:3)NATO as a “return to the European identity in security and defence”, involving a combination of a united Europe, limited US participation in NATO and none-too- focused perception of threats. (cid:16)(cid:3) NATO as a “gentlemen’s club”, involving a complete US absence, a dispersed or united Europe and common or divergent threat perception508.
