CONCLUSIONS The main aim of this study was to present the challenges calling for better cooperation between the EU and NATO in a new strategic context. In this connection, the Author: - Conducted a review of EU security and defence between the Second World War and the launch of the European Security Strategy in 2003, focusing attention on these main trends: * Defence integration characterised by definite reactivity towards immediate threats and external changes to the security environment; *NATO/EU cooperation characterised by a definite need for cooperation; *National sensitivity with regard to sovereignty characterised by retaining the key role of nation states in security and their absolute weight in decision making; - Compiled a theoretical model in which the security environment is an independent variable, while EU and NATO security and defence strategic papers are a dependent variable. Answering the research question as to what the characteristics of the current security environment are, the Author presents the complex, hybrid character of threats and the new strategic context in which agents have to operate; - Conducts: 1. An analysis of the economic, political, and institutional challenges facing the EU and NATO; 2. An analysis of cooperation and challenges to cooperation between the two alliances and showing the need for: *additional boosting of cooperation in capabilities; *a greater degree of integration, cooperation and hence complementary; *greater confidence and intelligence exchange; *a resolution of the issue between Cyprus and Turkey which blocks practical cooperation between NATO and the EU – Berlin Plus and beyond; *directing priority attention in strategic planning: issues of terrorism, energy security and free access to global commons (high seas, airspace, outer space, and cyberspace) and 3. Analyses of specific cases – Libya, Bulgaria, and Ukraine, showing: *the specifics of the threats from the south and east; *the lack of key EU capabilities; *possible new approaches to expanding the two entities (in the Black Sea region and the post- Soviet area – first through EU and then NATO membership; giving priority to NATO enlargement in the Western Balkans and EU strengthening through the Eastern Partnership with the stress on Ukraine, Moldova, and Georgia); - Empirically tested through a personal sociological survey the theoretical model, recommendations and conclusions, thesis and hypotheses in this monograph. Based on the above, the Author proves her postulate on the need for a strategic reassessment of the security environment and for a modernisation of the European Security Strategy through confirming the hypotheses that: (cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3) 508 Спигелере, С., Р. Кортеуег. “Военни въпроси”, „Бъдещето на НАТО“, 2006 <http://www.nato.int/docu/review/2006/ issue2/ bulgarian/military.html> [Spiegeleire and Rem Korteweg, The Future of NATO, 2006] (cid:3) 357 1. The security environment has changed. The system of international relations is very unpredictable. The security environment is characterised by: *a complex set of threats – asymmetric, hybrid, domestic and external, all highly interlinked, alongside risks containing new components – economic, financial, energy, environmental, social, or justice; *diverse perceptions and assessments of risks by EU members, the public, and EU and NATO decision makers. 2. There is a causal link between changes to the security environment and EU and NATO strategic papers, shown when almost 94 percent of those surveyed gave a positive answered to the question whether dynamic international processes, especially over the past three years, call for a strategic rethink of the security environment accompanied by changes in current EU and NATO security strategic papers. 3. The current security environment requires better cooperation between EU and NATO. Commenting on the EU as a global actor able to respond rapidly to new geostrategic challenges, 72 percent of respondents noted the need for close cooperation with NATO. All those surveyed noted the need to improve cooperation between the two entities, with the highest percentage noted the urgent need for more integration, compatible capabilities and complementary. The research main ideas and recommendations, beyond those empirically tested, could be summarised thus: 1. Three potential scenarios emerge for EU security and defence: *the EU optimises its abilities within NATO, thus becoming a second NATO pillar, while the question of Cyprus and Malta which are not in the Alliance, remains open, alongside that of neutral nations Austria, Sweden, Finland, Ireland, Switzerland, and Denmark which does not participate in the CSDP; *Military integration within the EU at “two speeds,” using the opportunity opened by Lisbon Treaty Article I-41.6 for permanent structured cooperation between member states. This cooperation requires that only countries with capabilities answering the high criteria of modern missions participate. It is linked with NATO cooperation, building capabilities, and more active inclusion of European states in the entire spectrum of Alliance missions. *Independent European army, begging the question whether they would follow the NATO model of national rather than joint armed forces with budget indicators, or else Jean Monnet and René Pleven’s 1950s vision of a supranational European defence community with *common authorities, armed forces, budget, *combat training systems and weaponry, exclusively for defending European territory. Which of the three potential CSDP scenarios develops depends on the three key formulas this research paper examines: the power formula – resources plus the desire and skill to deploy them, the movement formula – way, speed and time, and the decision sustainability formula – a clear strategic vision and political will at both the European and national levels and European public support. Each proposed scenario entails a set integration level. In view of the EU’s unique status of something like an international organisation, something like a federation, something “like nothing at all in the world,” 509 the study asks whether it is possible to position the EU entirely within an existing framework of integration models or whether an attempt ought to be made at a new framework for its development. 2. Emergence of two new modes of integration in the European project: evolutionary and adaptive. (cid:135)(cid:3) Evolutionary integration rests on the uniqueness of the EU and combines known integration elements with ones stemming from the absence of an analogy; (cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3)(cid:3) 509 Saroyan, W, Knife-like, Flower-like, like Nothing at all in the World, 1942 (cid:3) 358 (cid:135)(cid:3) Adaptive integration follows set events causing nations to realise their inability to cope individually. They thus discover the need for a common vision for the EU and form joint actions that determine the direction of integration and lend sustainability to the European project. When formulating potential scenarios for the future of the European project and the degree of integration within it, one of the most substantial components is “invisible”, which relates to values, beliefs and aspirations of both the public and EU decision makers. 3. Defining an idea to recognise the horizontal character of security policy and rethink the member state budgeting by including the element of security into budget items of diverse sectoral policies beyond home affairs, security and defence, viz. energy, the environment, the economy and finance, transport, science, education, youth policy, the arts, healthcare, tourism, agriculture, and social policy. Injecting security into the strategic papers of different sectoral policies would recognise its complex character while redistributing its budgetary burden in a balanced manner; 4. In the context of the monograph, defining conclusions which might serve in the process of Bulgarian preparations for chairing the EU Council in 2018: to make security part of the currently emerging priorities for 2018, alongside energy (energy security), the single digital market (cyber security); migration flows from the south and east and a strategic vision for beyond 2020. The analysis of presidencies between 2009 and 2013 as part of the research paper’ temporal scope shows that each included among its priorities an element relating to EU positioning on the international scene: something that ought to be taken into account in shaping the EU agenda for the future Bulgarian presidency in 2018; 5. Launching the idea of a European defence semester and stressing the currency of the Bulgarian proposal of a European defence white paper 510. Both ideas relate to EU member state defence budget and capability coordination. In turn, this ought to help the process of overcoming uncoordinated national cuts in EU defence and shortfalls in capability or capability duplication with NATO; 6. Listing the challenges stemming from different conceptual paradigms and leading to different approaches to security and international relations; 7. Formulating clear ambitions in a renewed strategic document presenting a smart security strategy. Launching the idea of a future smart EU security strategy featuring: *A common risk and threat assessment; *Proactiveness, anticipation and flexibility (timely adaptation) vis-à-vis the security environment; *Balanced “soft” and “hard” approaches; *Cooperation with NATO, but on the basis of the greatest prior coordination within the EU. J. Nye writes that “security is like oxygen: you tend not to notice it until you lose it” 511. The lack of a current EU security and defence strategy begs the question of EU ambitions: what player the EU wants to be, whether it wishes to deploy soft of hard power, how it interacts with NATO given both organisations share an operations theatre, what political maturity levels obtain in member states, and what is the public backing for CSDP development. Defining EU ambition levels, its strategic aims and military capabilities is of key importance for the EU’s future positioning in the global contest. Worsened conditions in the Middle East and North Africa should not throw doubts upon EU existence or upon its sui generis nature. The proposal entailed reviewing capabilities and drawing up a modernisation and optimisation action plan to make the EU equal to new realities. 511 Nye, J S, “East Asian Security: The Case for Deep Engagement,” Foreign Affairs July/August 1995 <https://www.foreignaffairs.com/articles/asia/1995-07-01/east-asian-security-case-deep- engagement> (cid:3) 359 mobilise political will and a shared strategic vision to adapt the EU to new realities, rather than denigrate or deface it. As distinct from other international players, the EU is the largest net aid contributor to third countries. The EU was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for its successful peaceful integration project. The very fact that today’s refugee wave is towards Europe, despite the immediate proximity of countries closer in character to refugees’ homelands, proves the EU’s value, advantages and accomplishments. The EU’s strengths should not be presented as weaknesses the so called “soft power.“ The deficit of set capabilities should rather be made up than ignored. This calls for modernising the European security strategy and imbuing it with a smart design that rises to new realities and challenges. In this the EU should be defined as a smart power, meaning a combination of hard and soft power to give effective strategies adapted to diverse situations and being proactive rather than merely reactive to changes in the security environment. Making the European project sustainable involves placing its development upon a strategic vision guaranteeing security, welfare and identity and offering sufficient adaptivity and reaction mechanisms in a security environment of exceptional complexity. Amid globalisation, the speed and time components are key to EU integration and development, and in particular to CSDP development. The road ahead for NATO and the EU, for their members, the speed and time they elect to traverse it, and whether they have a defined ultimate aim depends to a significant extent on the need for a strategic redefining of the security environment taking into account the current and new global threats and challenges in an interdependent world. “Certified translation from Bulgarian into English language”, Aglika Markova, Orchid-94 Ltd.
